title: Babylon Is Taken
sum: The longest oracle in the book opens: the word of the LORD against Babylon and the land of the Chaldeans. The city that took Judah captive is told its gods are shattered (50:2). A nation from the north comes against it, as Babylon once came from the north against Judah (50:3, 41-43). While Babylon falls, Israel and Judah come home together, weeping, asking the way to Zion and joining the LORD in a covenant they will not forget (50:4-5).

The poem moves back and forth between three scenes: the attack on Babylon, the home-coming of the scattered flock, and the reason for the verdict. Babylon is guilty of pride and of burning the temple (50:28-29), and the LORD, Israel's strong redeemer, will plead his people's case (50:34). The chapter ends with the lion from the Jordan and the shout, 'Babylon is seized!' (50:44-46).
readings: Read as a forecast of 539 BC

The oracle announces the fall of Babylon to a northern coalition and the release of the exiles, and it was fulfilled when Cyrus took the city in October 539 and allowed Judeans to go home in 538. Some details (total ruin, no one living there) did not happen at once and are read as fulfilled over centuries, as Babylon declined.

Many critical scholars hear a poem of the exile, made of older lines (50:40, 44-45 from the Edom oracle; 50:41-43 from Jeremiah 6; Isaiah 13) and shaped as hope for people who lived under Babylon's rule. It tells them that their masters are not permanent and that a return is certain.
Read as the reversal of Jeremiah's own book

Babylon was the instrument against Judah (25:9; 27:6), and the book now turns each judgment on Babylon: the foe from the north, the sword, the sheep devoured, the temple's vengeance. The book of judgment ends with a promise that judgment itself is limited.

views.H: The poem has no date inside it. 51:59-64 sets Jeremiah's scroll against Babylon in 594/593 BC, when Zedekiah's court was thinking of revolt. The fall it describes came in 539 BC, 55 years later. Cyrus did not destroy the city or kill its people (Nabonidus Chronicle; Cyrus Cylinder), so the oracle's pictures of total ruin are either poetic or fulfilled later: Darius I retook the city after revolts in 522 and 521, Xerxes punished it after revolts about 484, and Alexander, who entered it in 331 BC, planned to restore its temple.
views.C: Carroll, McKane and many others hold chapters 50-51 to be a later collection, partly because the poem's Babylon is already weak and the hope of return is close. Many lines are repeated from elsewhere in Jeremiah (6:22-24; 49:18-21) and from Isaiah 13-14. Lundbom and some others find a core in the prophet's own time. The Greek of chapter 50 (Greek 27) is shorter in places (for example, it lacks the line in 50:2) and reads differently elsewhere (for example, in 50:7).
views.J: Rashi (on 51:1) explains Leb-qamai as Kasdim in the atbash cipher and the 'destroying wind' as the king of Persia and Media; on 51:41 he reads Sheshach as Babel. Jewish readers set the oracle inside the seventy years of Babylon's rule (25:12; 29:10), after which Israel returns.
views.X: Christians read the fall of Babylon as God's judgment on a persecuting empire and as the pattern for Revelation 14, 17 and 18, which take over the cry 'Fallen, fallen' (Isaiah 21:9; Jeremiah 50:2; 51:8), the call 'Come out of her' (51:45) and the stone thrown into the river (51:63-64; Revelation 18:21). The return of the exiles under Cyrus is the first fulfillment of the hope; the church sees a fuller one in Christ.
views.F: Futurist interpreters read 50-51 as unfulfilled in part, since Babylon was not left uninhabited in 539 and the description is of total, permanent desolation. They expect a future rebuilding and a final destruction of Babylon (compare Revelation 17-18). Others answer that Jeremiah's language of permanent ruin was fulfilled by Babylon's gradual decline and abandonment.

deep.h: The Hebrew and the Greek of the Babylon oracle
deep.b:
In the Greek Jeremiah the oracle against Babylon is chapters 27-28, after the oracle against Egypt (Greek 26) and before the oracle on the Philistines (Greek 29). The Greek of chapter 50 is shorter than the Hebrew in many small places. A few examples: the heading lacks 'the land of the Chaldeans' and 'by Jeremiah the prophet' (50:1); 'the LORD declares' is missing in 50:10 and 50:35; and the line about images and idols is missing in 50:2. Entries in the variants list the larger differences. Where it matters, the Greek reads different words: 'the one who gathered their fathers' for the LORD as 'hope of their ancestors' (50:7), and the 'Greek sword' for 'the oppressor's sword' (50:16). The Greek translator also turned the place names Merathaim and Pekod into words (50:21).

Only one Qumran copy preserves any of chapters 50-52: 4QJer-e (4Q72b), with parts of 50:4-6. In the Abegg-Bowley-Cook transcription it agrees with the Masoretic Text apart from spelling (for example 'it has become', 50:6) and one place in 50:4, where 'in the days' is missing and 'those' follows 'at that time' (see the variant). Wherever this part says 'the Greek', it means Swete's printed text of Codex Vaticanus (with Swete's chapter and verse numbers); Ziegler's critical edition was not used for these chapters. For the Hebrew of 50-52 the base is the Leningrad Codex. Rashi was read in Sefaria's text (on 51:1 and 51:41); other commentators are cited as reported in the sources listed.

The Babylonian Nabonidus Chronicle says the army of Cyrus defeated the Babylonian army at Opis in September 539, took Sippar without a battle on 14 Tashritu, and on 16 Tashritu (12 October) Ugbaru, the governor of Gutium, entered Babylon 'without battle'. Cyrus himself entered on 3 Arahsamnu (29 October) and the Cyrus Cylinder says he came in peace and restored the gods to their shrines. Herodotus (1.191) and Xenophon (Cyropaedia 7.5) add the story that Cyrus diverted the Euphrates into a canal and entered by the river bed during a festival. The chronicle is silent on this, and historians are divided on it. The Bible's picture of 'drought on her waters' (50:38) and 'the fords seized' (51:32) fits that story, but it also fits ordinary siege language. The Book of Daniel puts the end on the night of Belshazzar's feast (Daniel 5:30).

The oracle describes slaughter, ruin and an uninhabited waste. The city was not wrecked in 539. Babylon revolted against Darius I in 522 and 521 and was retaken, and again under Xerxes in 484 or so. Alexander found it a great city in 331. It declined after the Seleucids built Seleucia on the Tigris. Readers handle the difference in three ways: the language is poetic; the prophecy was fulfilled in stages over centuries; or the fulfillment is still future.

settings.by: The LORD, through Jeremiah the prophet (50:1)
settings.to: Judah's exiles in Babylon and those still in Judah, and through them the nations. By the heading, Jeremiah gave it to Seraiah to read in Babylon (51:59-64).
settings.when: The heading has no date. The book places the scroll in Zedekiah's fourth year (594/593 BC). The fall it describes came in 539 BC, 55 years later. Critical scholars date the poems to the exile, perhaps about 550-539.
settings.why: Jeremiah had told the exiles to settle, marry and 'seek the welfare of the city' for seventy years (29:5-7, 10). This oracle tells them the other half: that Babylon is not forever, that the LORD will call it to account for burning his temple, and that a return will come. For people ruled by an empire that looked unbeatable, it makes the empire's fall a certainty before it happens.
settings.readers: The exiles and their children who read the collected book in Babylon and, after 538 BC, in Judah. They saw the oracle as the word of Jeremiah being kept. Persian-period readers could read it with Cyrus's victory in view.
views: Traditional and some modern readers: Jeremiah, who gave a scroll against Babylon to Seraiah (51:59-64), left these oracles written down.
Many critical scholars: the oracles were composed or expanded in the exile, in the years before Cyrus, from older material, and attached to Jeremiah's name.

settings.to: The exiles of both kingdoms, the northern kingdom taken in 722 BC and Judah in 597 and 586 BC
settings.when: In the days when Babylon falls
settings.why: To tell the scattered people that the division between Israel and Judah ends in the return, and that the wrongs of shepherds and enemies will not decide the end. The people are not told to go back at once: they are told that they will ask the way and join the LORD in a covenant.
settings.readers: Exiles who read it as a promise that the lost tribes and Judah would be one again.

settings.when: When the northern army is on its way
settings.why: On the exilic reading, to warn those who had settled in Babylon (29:5-7) to leave before the attack and to lead the way home, like goats in front of the flock. It is the first of four calls to flee (50:8; 51:6, 45, 50).
settings.readers: Later exiles who stayed in Babylon after 538 BC and needed the same word (Zechariah 2:6-7).

settings.why: To assure captives who are 'crushed down' that God, as redeemer, will act as the family that buys back a relative, and as a lawyer who wins the case. The words are about the LORD, whose name is 'the LORD of Armies', not about a human champion.
settings.readers: Exiles for whom redemption was the great word of the return.

title: The Cup, the Club and the Stone
sum: The oracle against Babylon goes on in a flood of images. The LORD stirs up a destroying wind (51:1-4). Babylon, the gold cup that made the earth drunk, falls (51:7-8). The Medes are roused; the LORD, who made the earth and sees through idols, uses Babylon as a war club and then breaks it (51:11-26). Nations are called to arms from Ararat, Minni and Ashkenaz (51:27-33). Zion speaks and the LORD answers (51:34-40).

The last third calls the exiles to leave (51:45-53) and describes the end (51:54-58). The chapter closes with a story: in 594/593 BC Jeremiah gave a scroll about Babylon to Seraiah, Baruch's brother, to read in Babylon, tie to a stone and throw into the Euphrates (51:59-64). 'Up to this point are the words of Jeremiah.'
readings: The voice changes: the LORD, a crowd of nations, Zion, the escaped fugitives and the prophet speak in turn. Many scholars hear a liturgy or an anthology of songs of vengeance and hope. Its hard lines about vengeance are the voice of victims who give their anger to God.
Read as the end of an empire

The poem names real peoples (Medes, Ararat, Minni, Ashkenaz) and real objects (the walls, the river, the gate) and forecasts the end of Babylon's rule. Historians compare it with the Nabonidus Chronicle and Herodotus.
Read as a pattern for the end

Revelation 14, 17 and 18 borrow the cup, the call to leave, the rejoicing heavens and the stone thrown into water, and build 'Babylon the Great' from them. Seen this way, Babylon is the name for any great city that kills God's people and lives off the earth.

views.H: The Medes (51:11, 28) were not the army that took Babylon in 539: that was the Persian Cyrus, who had absorbed the Median kingdom about 550. The oracle's 'kings of Media' fits the years just before 539 when Median and Persian forces were one. Seraiah's journey in 594/593 BC (51:59) belongs to a time of unrest in the empire and to Zedekiah's wish to show loyalty.
views.C: The poem's lines are drawn from earlier prophets: 51:15-19 is 10:12-16; 51:58 resembles Habakkuk 2:13; 50:39-40 resembles Isaiah 13:19-22. The Greek omits 51:44b-49a (about 110 words) and the cipher Sheshach, and ends 51:64 without the closing note. Tov and others take the Greek to represent an earlier, shorter edition.
views.J: Rashi reads Leb-qamai (51:1) and Sheshach (51:41) as atbash ciphers, citing the Midrash Tanchuma for Sheshach, and explains the 'destroying wind' as the spirit of the king of Persia and Media. Jewish readers set the fall within the seventy years of Babylon's rule (25:12; 29:10).
views.X: Revelation 18:4, 'Come out of her, my people', quotes this chapter's call (51:45). Revelation 18:21 repeats Seraiah's stone, with a millstone thrown into the sea. Tertullian already read the Babylon of Revelation as Rome (Against Marcion 3.13), and Augustine read it as the earthly city opposed to the city of God (City of God 18.2); later traditions applied the name to the papacy or to a rebuilt Babylon (see the card below).
views.F: Dispensational and some other futurist interpreters expect a rebuilt Babylon on the Euphrates and a final destruction in the last days, taking 51:26, 37, 43 literally and noting that Babylon was never left uninhabited in the Persian conquest. Others read the cup and the call to leave as symbols for the whole system of the world, not a place.

deep.b:
Two names in this chapter are written in atbash, a cipher that swaps the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet with the last, the second with the second from last, and so on. 'Sheshach' (51:41; also 25:26) is Babel; 'Leb-qamai' (51:1) is Kasdim, 'Chaldeans'. Rashi says both. The Greek translation omits Sheshach in both places and has 'Chaldeans' for Leb-qamai, so the translator may have solved the cipher, dropped it, or worked from a text without it.

Why the ciphers are used is unknown. The Plain gives the Hebrew sounds and explains them in notes.

deep.h: The gold cup, Babylon, and Revelation
deep.b:
In 51:7 Babylon is a gold cup in the LORD's hand: beautiful, rich, and poison for the nations that drank from it. In Jeremiah 25:15-29 the LORD gives the nations a cup of wine of wrath. Revelation 17:4 gives the woman Babylon a gold cup in her hand 'full of disgusting things'. In Revelation 14:8 and Revelation 18:3 the nations drink her wine. John uses Jeremiah's image of an empire that made the world drunk with its power and wealth.

Revelation's other borrowings from this chapter: the 'many waters' on which she sits (Jeremiah 51:13; Revelation 17:1), the call to leave (Jeremiah 51:45; Revelation 18:4), heaven rejoicing (Jeremiah 51:48; Revelation 18:20), and the stone thrown into the Euphrates (Jeremiah 51:63-64; Revelation 18:21). Revelation has a city and an empire in mind that its first readers would name Rome (Revelation 17:9 speaks of seven hills or mountains).
deep.refs: Jeremiah 51:7; Jeremiah 51:13; Jeremiah 51:45; Jeremiah 51:63-64; Revelation 14:8; Revelation 17:1-4; Revelation 18:4; Revelation 18:21

deep.b:
The chapter's ending is a story, in prose, in the third person: Jeremiah gave Seraiah son of Neriah, an officer on the king's staff, a scroll in which he had written 'all the disaster that was coming on Babylon'. In Babylon Seraiah was to read it aloud, say a prayer, tie a stone to it and throw it into the Euphrates, saying that Babylon would sink the same way. It is a sign-act like the belt hidden at the Euphrates (13:1-11) or the broken jar (19:1-13), with a twist: it is done by someone else, in the enemy city, with no audience but the LORD (and perhaps Jewish exiles).

The date, the fourth year of Zedekiah, is the year of the yoke of chapters 27-28 and of Hananiah's false prophecy. A journey 'with' Zedekiah or 'from' Zedekiah (the Hebrew and the Greek differ) fits a diplomatic mission to Nebuchadnezzar. Jeremiah 29:3 mentions another embassy at about this time. The story shows that Jeremiah, who counseled submission to Babylon, never forgot its fall. It may also be the editors' way to fix the poems of 50-51 to the prophet's name.

traditions.q: Is the 'Babylon' of Jeremiah 50-51 and Revelation 17-18 a church? (This is mainly a question about Revelation, which takes over Jeremiah's Babylon.)
views: Luther used 'Babylon' for the papal church: 'The Babylonian Captivity of the Church' (1520) says the sacraments were held captive by Rome, and the Smalcald Articles (1537) name the pope the Antichrist.

The Westminster Confession of Faith 25.6 (1646) said the pope of Rome is the antichrist and man of sin, and Revelation's Babylon was often read as papal Rome in the Reformed tradition. The American Presbyterian revision of 1787-89 (adopted 1788) dropped that clause; other Reformed bodies kept it.

The Second London Baptist Confession (1689), 26.4, says the pope of Rome can in no sense be head of the church but is 'that antichrist, that man of sin, and son of perdition'. Not every Baptist body holds the 1689 Confession.

The Catholic Church does not teach that Babylon is the church. Catholic commentary reads Babylon in Revelation as the Rome of the emperors, a persecuting world power. Augustine already called Rome a second Babylon in the line of the earthly city (City of God 18.2). The Catechism's teaching on the Antichrist (CCC 675-677) speaks of a final religious deception and does not name the papacy.
Walvoord (1966) took Revelation 17 as a world religious system and Revelation 18 as a rebuilt literal city of Babylon on the Euphrates that is destroyed in the end time.

Ellen White's The Great Controversy (1888) reads Babylon in Revelation 14 and 18 as apostate Christianity, led by Rome and joined by fallen Protestantism, and 'Come out of her' as the last call to leave it.

settings.by: The LORD, through Jeremiah the prophet; at the end of 51:59-64 the story says Jeremiah wrote it in one scroll
settings.to: Exiles of Judah, and the nations that Babylon ruled
settings.when: Like chapter 50, undated; the book sets the scroll in 594/593 BC (51:59) and the fall in 539 BC
settings.why: To make the case that Babylon will be repaid for the temple and for the nations it crushed (51:11, 24, 35, 49), to call the LORD's people out of the city, and to answer Zion's complaint (51:34-35) with the LORD's promise to plead her case (51:36). The idol passage (51:15-19) says why a power with gods of metal cannot stand.
settings.readers: Exiles in Babylon and their descendants, the first readers of the collected book. Later churches read it against any great imperial power.
views: The traditional view: the poems come from the prophet, read in Babylon by Seraiah.
Critical scholars: the poems are exilic, in the years of Cyrus, built on Jeremiah's earlier oracles.

settings.what: Zion's complaint and the LORD's answer
settings.by: Zion and Jerusalem (51:34-35), then the LORD (51:36-40)
settings.to: The LORD, and the exiles overhearing
settings.when: After the fall of Jerusalem, in the exile
settings.why: A lament gives words to the exiles' grievance: Nebuchadnezzar swallowed Zion like a sea monster. The LORD's answer takes the case ('I am pleading your case') and makes Babylon the victim of a banquet and a slaughter. The hearers are given the right to ask for justice.
settings.readers: The exiles and later readers of the collected book, for whom Zion's cry and the LORD's answer gave words for the loss of the city and temple.

settings.when: Before and as the city falls
settings.why: To tell the exiles to leave before the fall and not lose heart at the rumors of war in the empire. The point is not to move on a day but to keep faith: 'remember the LORD from far off, and let Jerusalem rise in your heart' (51:50).
settings.readers: Exiles of the Persian period who needed to decide whether to go home; and Christian readers of Revelation 18:4.

settings.what: Seraiah's mission and the scroll thrown in the Euphrates
settings.to: Seraiah son of Neriah, Baruch's brother, an officer on the royal staff, on a journey to Babylon
settings.when: The fourth year of Zedekiah (594/593 BC)
settings.why: A sign-act. Jeremiah's words against Babylon were to be read in Babylon, then sunk with a stone. The act shows that the LORD's word against Babylon is as good as done, in the same year that Jeremiah was telling Judah to obey Nebuchadnezzar (27:12). Reading it at Babylon, the capital of the king whom Judah feared, gave Seraiah's mission the weight of a prayer.
settings.readers: Exiles and later readers who read of it as proof that Jeremiah's call to submit was not loyalty to Babylon but patience until the LORD acted.
views: The Hebrew: Seraiah went in the king's party to Babylon.
The Greek: Seraiah went from the king, as his envoy.

title: The City Burned and the King Freed
sum: The book ends with history. Chapter 52 tells again the last years of Judah: the reign of Zedekiah (52:1-3), the siege of Jerusalem, its breach and the capture of the king (52:4-11), the burning of the temple and the carrying off of its bronze (52:12-23), the execution of the leaders at Riblah (52:24-27), the count of the exiles (52:28-30), and, thirty-seven years after the first exile, the release of King Jehoiachin from prison (52:31-34).

Most of the chapter is the same Hebrew as 2 Kings 24:18-25:30. It leaves out the story of Gedaliah (2 Kings 25:22-26), which Jeremiah 40-41 has told, and adds the long list of temple furnishings, the officials killed at Riblah, and the exile numbers. It ends not with Jeremiah's fate but with a small light: a king of David's line eating at a king's table.
readings: Jeremiah had warned that the king, the temple and the city would fall. Chapter 52 shows it happening, with dates and numbers. The prophet of 'destruction' was right, and that gave his words about restoration their weight.
Read as a note of hope

The book ends with Jehoiachin freed and fed. For the exiles it was a sign that the line of David was alive. Readers have taken it as a small seed of hope (compare Jeremiah 24:5-7; 29:10-14) or as only a note that the exile continued (Noth).
The closing note of 51:64 sets chapter 52 outside Jeremiah's own words. It was added by editors from the history of Kings, and the Greek and Hebrew copies of Jeremiah handle it differently.

views.H: The dates here are among the best fixed in the Bible: the siege began on 15 January 588 BC, the city was breached in July 586, and the temple burned in August 586. Some scholars date the fall in 587. The last date, the release of Jehoiachin, falls in spring 561 BC, the year Amel-Marduk (Evil-merodach) took the throne. Ration tablets from Babylon name 'Ya'ukin, king of Yahudu'.
views.C: Many scholars take Jeremiah 52 as drawn from Kings (or from a source Kings also used), with additions: the detailed list of vessels (52:17-23, fuller than 2 Kings 25:13-17), the officials at Riblah (52:10), the counts of exiles (52:28-30) and the detail that Zedekiah was held in prison until he died (52:11). The Greek lacks verses 2-3, 15, 27b and 28-30, and a few numbers differ.
views.J: The Ninth of Av is the Jewish fast that remembers the burning of the temple, and the Talmud discusses the dates of the burning, the seventh, ninth and tenth of Av (Taanit 29a; see the note on 52:12). The reading from the Prophets for that day is Jeremiah 8:13-9:23, not chapter 52. The tradition that Jeremiah wrote Kings (Bava Batra 15a) fits the shared ending of the two books.
views.X: Christians see in the burning of the temple and the survival of Jehoiachin's line the situation into which Matthew places the genealogy of Jesus: 'Jeconiah' and the exile are the hinge of Matthew 1:11-12. Jehoiachin's release is read as a small sign that David's line was not cut off.
views.F: Some futurist readers see here the start of the 'times of the Gentiles', the long period of foreign rule over Jerusalem that Jesus names in Luke 21:24. The Temple's loss is the first of two destructions (586 BC, AD 70).

deep.h: Why does Jeremiah end this way?
deep.b:
Three explanations are given. (1) To show the word fulfilled. The chapter gives, with dates and numbers, the events Jeremiah foretold (the temple objects, Zedekiah's end, the leaders at Riblah). (2) To keep a hope. Jehoiachin's release repeats the ending of Kings and ends the book with a living son of David, after Jeremiah 22:24-30 had said none of his sons would rule. (3) To join two books. The Talmud says Jeremiah wrote Kings (Bava Batra 15a), which would explain why the two end together; many modern scholars think an editor copied Kings to give Jeremiah a closing historical frame.

Chronicles ends differently: with the decree of Cyrus quoting Jeremiah's seventy years (2 Chronicles 36:22-23). The two endings differ: Kings looks from the low point, and Chronicles from the first step home.

Clay tablets found in the ruins of Babylon, published by Ernst Weidner in 1939, are lists of rations of oil and grain given to people at the royal court. They include 'Ya'ukin, king of the land of Yahudu' and five sons, among craftsmen and officials from many conquered lands. At least one is dated to 592 BC. They show that Babylon treated Jehoiachin as a royal captive and fed him from the state stores, and that Judeans in exile dated their years by his exile (Ezekiel 1:2). The 37th year (561 BC) and the accession of Evil-merodach are consistent with the Babylonian records, which put Amel-Marduk on the throne in 562.

settings.what: The fall of Jerusalem retold, with its sequel
settings.by: An editor, on the critical view; Jewish tradition gives the whole book to Jeremiah (Bava Batra 15a). The book itself says 'Up to this point are the words of Jeremiah' (51:64).
settings.to: Exiles in Babylon and later readers of the collected book
settings.when: After the last event in it, the release of Jehoiachin in 561 BC; the editing could be any time after that
settings.why: To close the book with the events it foretold, in a form its readers already knew from Kings, so that the prophet's word is seen to be kept. It adds items that help a reader who was in exile: the temple bronze that was carried to Babylon, the people who were taken, and the king who was finally freed.
settings.readers: The exiles and their descendants, who needed a summary of what had happened and why, and a sign that David's line had not ended.
views: Many critical scholars: the editor of Jeremiah copied Kings with additions.
Some scholars: Jeremiah and Kings both used an earlier account.

settings.by: A record of the exiles, quoted by the editor
settings.to: Readers who wanted to know how many Judeans were taken, and when
settings.when: Three deportations in Nebuchadnezzar's seventh, eighteenth and twenty-third years (598/597, 587/586 and 582/581 BC)
settings.why: To keep a record that the exiles were a real, countable part of the nation. The numbers are far lower than 2 Kings 24:14, 16 and may be a separate count, perhaps of men only. The year numbers do not match Kings either (see the note on 52:28).
settings.readers: Exiles, who knew whose families were taken in which wave.

settings.when: In the thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's exile, the first year of Evil-merodach (spring 561 BC)
settings.why: To show that the line of David was not ended: a son of David, after thirty-seven years in prison, is brought to the king's table. It is the final fact in the book, with no promise attached.
settings.readers: Judean exiles for whom the kingship of David was at stake.
views: Jehoiachin's release prepares for the return and for the Davidic hope (Jeremiah 23:5-6; 33:14-17).
Jehoiachin remains a captive at a foreign court (Noth).
